O que é um verbo? O teste do \"acontecer: What is a verb? The "happening" test

What is a verb? The "happening" test. Before any table, the basic question: what is a verb? A verb is the word that expresses an action, a state or an occurrence. It is what a person does, is or experiences. And there is a reliable test to recognise it, the "happening" test: "I ___ at home." → live, am, stay → verb. "He ___ Russian." → speaks, studies, learns → verb. "We ___ books." → read, buy, write → verb. The verb is the backbone of the sentence. Without a verb there is no action. Without a verb there is no complete sentence. You already know how to say "Э́то но́вый дом" (this is a new house). But you cannot yet say "I am building a new house" or "He lives in a new house". That is the subject of this lesson. And the good news? The Russian verb is much more regular than you think. Much more than the noun or the adjective. The exceptions are few, and the rules are consistent. You will see.
O que é um pronome pessoal do caso reto?: What is a subject pronoun? (the simple truth, no fear). Before you conjugate any verb, you need to know what it is conjugated with. That means knowing the subject pronouns. "Subject pronoun" may sound like a grammar monster, but it is the simplest thing in the world. Let me take the name apart: Pronoun = a word that replaces a noun. Instead of "John" you say "he". Instead of "Mary" you say "she". Subject = it is the doer of the action in the sentence. In English, the subject pronouns are: In Russian, they are: That is all. You have used "I, you, he, she" all your life. Russian is the same: you only have to learn the matching words. No terror, no absurd memorising. Five minutes of attention is enough. Important details: • 1. Ты vs. вы. In Russian, ты is used with friends, family, children and close people. Вы is used with strangers, older people, authorities, and always for the plural. English has only "you" for both, so you must choose. • 2. Он, она́, оно́. In Russian, everything has a gender, even objects. So "table" (стол) is masculine → он; "house" (дом) is masculine → он; "book" (кни́га) is feminine → она́; "window" (окно́) is neuter → оно́. English says "it" for all of these. This is scary at first, but you already learned in lesson 11 that gender is determined by the last letter. Now you just apply it: if the noun is masculine, use он; if feminine, она́; if neuter, оно́. • 3. Они́. A single form for all three genders in the plural. It does not matter whether it is "they" (men) or "they" (women). It is always они́.
O que é conjugação? (a explicação mais c: What is conjugation? (the clearest explanation you will read)

What is conjugation? (the clearest explanation you will read). Before anything else, a question nobody asks and everybody should: what does it mean to conjugate a verb? To conjugate is to change the form of the verb to match the subject of the sentence. English does this very little (I speak, he speaks); Russian does it for every person. Look: Notice that the stem speak- is always the same. Only the ending changes (here just -s in the third person). You never thought "I invented a new stem" when you wrote "speaks". You just changed the ending. That is conjugating. Russian works on exactly the same principle. You have a stem (which carries the meaning) and an ending (which carries the person). The stem never changes. The ending changes. ЧИТА- + -Ю = чита́ю (I read) ЧИТА- + -ЕШЬ = чита́ешь (you read) ЧИТА- + -ЕТ = чита́ет (he / she reads) ЧИТА- + -ЕМ = чита́ем (we read) ЧИТА- + -ЕТЕ = чита́ете (you read, plural or formal) ЧИТА- + -ЮТ = чита́ют (they read) The stem ЧИТА- never changed. Only the ending. Always. The difference from English is that Russian has a different ending for every person, and that is what scares beginners. But the mechanics are simple. You have just learned to conjugate a Russian verb. That is it. The rest is practice.
A \"tesourinha do verbo\": o método que: The verb "scissors": the method nobody teaches. Just as we did with the adjective (lesson 12), we will apply the scissors to the verb. Remember this: every Russian verb is a LEGO of two pieces: STEM (untouchable) + ENDING (movable). And the method is always the same: • 1. Find the infinitive (the "dictionary" form, which ends in -ТЬ, -ТИ or -ЧЬ). • 2. Cut off the infinitive ending (-ТЬ, -ТИ, -ЧЬ). You have the stem. • 3. Paste on the personal ending (-Ю, -ЕШЬ, -ЕТ, -ЕМ, -ЕТЕ, -ЮТ or -Ю, -ИШЬ, -ИТ, -ИМ, -ИТЕ, -ЯТ). Done. The verb is conjugated. See it in practice with чита́ть (to read): • 1. Infinitive: чита́ть • 2. Cut -ТЬ: чита́ (stem) • 3. Paste the endings: чита́ + ю = чита́ю (I read) чита́ + ешь = чита́ешь (you read) чита́ + ет = чита́ет (he reads) чита́ + ем = чита́ем (we read) чита́ + ете = чита́ете (you read, plural or formal) чита́ + ют = чита́ют (they read) And with говори́ть (to speak): • 1. Infinitive: говори́ть • 2. Cut -ТЬ: говори́- • 3. Paste the endings: говор + ю = говорю́ (I speak) говори́ + шь = говори́шь (you speak) говори́ + т = говори́т (he speaks) говори́ + м = говори́м (we speak) говори́ + те = говори́те (you speak, plural or formal) говор + ят = говоря́т (they speak). Notice: in the verb говори́ть, the vowel -и- stays in most forms (говор-и-шь) but disappears before -ю and -ят (говор-ю, говор-ят). That is normal. Why does this help? Because the Russian verb works like LEGO: instead of memorising the table, you learn to build each form. The Russian infinitive: three endings. In Russian, the infinitive (the "dictionary" form) ends in three different ways: The good news: you do not need to worry about -ТИ and -ЧЬ now. They are a minority. The vast majority of verbs end in -ТЬ, and that is what we study in this lesson.
O infinitivo russo: as três terminações: The Russian infinitive: the three endings
As duas conjugações: a lógica por trás: The two conjugations: the logic behind them
The two conjugations: the logic behind them. Here is a point that tends to stay unclear. Let us clear it up. In Russian, verbs fall into two conjugations. And the difference between them is in the personal endings: 1st CONJUGATION: 2nd CONJUGATION: How do you decide which conjugation to use? Look at the ending of the infinitive: Verbs in -ать and -ять → almost always 1st conjugation. Verbs in -ить → almost always 2nd conjugation. Verbs in -еть → mostly 2nd (смотреть, видеть, сидеть), with exceptions such as болеть and уметь. Examples: чита́ть (to read) → ends in -ать → 1st conjugation → чита́ю, чита́ешь, чита́ет... гуля́ть (to take a walk) → -ять → 1st conjugation → гуля́ю, гуля́ешь, гуля́ет... боле́ть (to be ill) → -еть → 1st conjugation (an exception) → боле́ю, боле́ешь, боле́ет... говори́ть (to speak) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → говорю́, говори́шь, говори́т... люби́ть (to love) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → люблю́, лю́бишь, лю́бит... звони́ть (to phone) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → звоню́, звони́шь, звони́т... Careful: there are exceptions. Some verbs in -ать, -ять, -еть belong to the 2nd conjugation. There are only eleven, and I will list them later.
Conjugar é mudar o final do verbo para m: To conjugate is to change the end of the verb to show WHO does the action: I speak, you speak, he speaks. English only changes the verb in the third person singular (speak → speaks). Russian changes it for every person. The Russian present tense has only TWO conjugations, and each has its own endings. Step by step: (1) drop the -ть from the infinitive to find the stem; (2) find out the conjugation of the verb; (3) add the six endings. 1st conjugation: -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют (after a consonant, -у and -ут). 2nd conjugation: -ю, -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят (after ж, ч, ш, щ, -у and -ат). The difference is in the vowel: е in the 1st, и in the 2nd.
o infinitivo português já mostra o grupo: an English infinitive («to speak») tells you nothing about the endings. The Russian infinitive in -ть alone is not enough either: you must learn the conjugation together with the verb; the next session gives the practical rules.
andar, ir (habitual): to walk, to go (on foot, habitually)

Os quatro tipos de verbo no presente: The four types of verb in the present
Os quatro tipos de verbo no presente. Pa: The four types of verb in the present. To make them easier to memorise, let's sort the present-tense verbs into four types. Type 1: ЗНАТЬ (the most common). Verbs in -ать and -ять (plus a few in -еть, such as уметь) that take the endings -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют. Type 2: ГОВОРИТЬ (verbs in -ить and most verbs in -еть). They take the endings -ю, -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят. Type 1B: ЖИТЬ (verbs whose stem ends in a consonant). They take endings similar to the first conjugation, but with -у in the first person singular (instead of -ю). Attention: when the stress falls on the ending, the letter е becomes ё (живёшь, живёт, живём, живёте). That does not change the ending, only the pronunciation; it is a spelling convention. Type 2B: irregular verbs (few, but important). хоте́ть (to want): хочу́, хо́чешь, хо́чет, хоти́м, хоти́те, хотя́т. This verb is a mixture of both conjugations. есть (to eat): ем, ешь, ест, еди́м, еди́те, едя́т. пить (to drink): пью, пьёшь, пьёт, пьём, пьёте, пьют. дать (to give): дам, дашь, даст, дади́м, дади́те, даду́т. English has almost no verb endings (only -s in "he works"), so Russian looks heavy at first. The good news: there are only two main sets of endings, and you can choose between them by looking at the infinitive.

A tip: almost all of these verbs have a connotation of perception (see, hear, look, breathe) or feeling (hate, offend, endure). It is not an absolute rule, but it helps. Memorise them.

O verbo SER (быть): a ausência mais famo: The verb TO BE (быть): the most famous absence in Russian

The verb TO BE (быть): the most famous absence in Russian. This is the biggest surprise for English speakers. Pay attention. In Russian, the verb TO BE (быть) does not exist in the present tense. In English we say: I am Brazilian. He is a doctor. We are students. In Russian, the verb disappears: Я брази́лец. (I Brazilian.) Он врач. (He doctor.) Мы студе́нты. (We students.) The verb "to be" simply does not appear. The context does its job. It is as if the sentence were "I Brazilian", "He doctor". Russian does not miss it at all. But note one exception: the 3rd person singular of быть — есть — survives with a special meaning: "there is", "exists", "has". This is the form you will use in the construction for "to have" (next section).
Como dizer \"eu tenho\", \"você tem\", \: How to say "I have", "you have", "he has"

How to say "I have", "you have", "he has". This is one of the biggest differences between English and Russian, and one of the first things you will want to say. Pay attention. In everyday Russian there is no verb "to have" like the English one. Instead, Russian uses a construction that, translated literally, means "by me there is": У меня́ есть кни́га. = I have a book. (Literally: "By me there is a book".) Let me take the formula apart: У = a preposition meaning "by", "at the place of", "in the possession of". меня́ = "me" (a special form of the pronoun "I" used after у). есть = "there is", "exists" (the surviving form of the verb to be). кни́га = "book" (the thing possessed). The structure is always the same. See it with all the pronouns: Notice how the pronoun changes after у: Why does it change? It is a grammar matter you will understand later, when we study the cases. For now, memorise the forms as a formula. That is how it is said. Full stop. The good news: the formula is fixed. Always у + special form + есть + object. No mystery. Can the word "есть" be left out? Yes, in informal contexts or when the possession is obvious: У меня́ кни́га. (I have a book.) У тебя́ вре́мя? (Do you have time?) But in general, use есть while you are learning. Russians understand perfectly and you will not risk sounding odd. How to negate: To say "I don't have", Russian uses нет instead of есть: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (I don't have a book.) У тебя́ нет вре́мени? (Don't you have time?) У него́ нет маши́ны. (He doesn't have a car.) Careful: the word after нет changes form. That is a subject for a future lesson. For now, memorise the most common examples: The logic is: when affirmative, use есть + the normal object; when negative, use нет + a "modified" object. You will learn how to modify it later, but you can already memorise these ready-made formulas.
Complete sentences: the first dialogues. Now that you know the subject pronouns, the two conjugations, the absence of the verb to be and the construction for "to have", you can form complete sentences. Dialogue 1 — In class: — Что ты де́лаешь? (What are you doing?) — Я чита́ю кни́гу. (I am reading a book.) — А он? (And he?) — Он пи́шет упражне́ние. (He is writing an exercise.) — А они́? (And they?) — Они́ говоря́т по-ру́сски. (They are speaking Russian.) Dialogue 2 — At home: — Где ты живёшь? (Where do you live?) — Я живу́ в Москве́. (I live in Moscow.) — А твоя́ семья́? (And your family?) — Они́ живу́т в Санкт-Петербу́рге. (They live in St Petersburg.) Dialogue 3 — At work: — Кто э́то? (Who is this?) — Э́то мой друг. Он рабо́тает здесь. (This is my friend. He works here.) — Он зна́ет ру́сский язы́к? (Does he know Russian?) — Да, немно́го. (Yes, a little.) Dialogue 4 — The verb "to have": — У тебя́ есть вре́мя? (Do you have time?) — Да, есть. А что? (Yes, I do. Why?) — У меня́ есть вопро́с. (I have a question.) — Хорошо́, спра́шивай. (All right, ask.) Dialogue 5 — Introducing yourself: — Приве́т! Как тебя́ зову́т? (Hi! What is your name?) — Меня́ зову́т Ива́н. А тебя́? (My name is Ivan. And yours?) — Меня́ зову́т Мари́я. Я изуча́ю ру́сский язы́к. (My name is Maria. I study Russian.) — Я то́же изуча́ю ру́сский. (I also study Russian.) Note: "Как тебя́ зову́т?" literally means "How do they call you?": the verb звать (to call) is in the 3rd person plural. The answer is Меня́ зову́т... ("They call me..."). It is the fixed formula for "What is your name?" in Russian. Memorise it as a block.
Como reconhecer a conjugação pelo infini: How to recognise the conjugation from the infinitive
Regras práticas: verbos em -ить são da 2: Practical rules: verbs in -ить are 2nd conjugation (говорить, любить, платить). Verbs in -еть are almost all 2nd conjugation (смотреть, видеть, сидеть), with exceptions such as «уметь» (умею) and «хотеть» (mixed). Verbs in -ать and -ять are almost all 1st conjugation (читать, делать, гулять), except a few 2nd-conjugation exceptions: слышать, держать, дышать, лежать, стоять. Verbs in -овать and -евать are 1st conjugation and change to -ую (рисовать → рисую). Verbs in -авать are 1st conjugation (вставать → встаю). In the 2nd conjugation, some consonants change ONLY in the «я» form: б → бл (любить → люблю), в → вл (готовить → готовлю), д → ж (видеть → вижу), т → ч (платить → плачу), с → ш (просить → прошу). The other forms stay regular: любишь, видишь.

— OS ADVÉRBIOS: as palavras que nunca mu: ADVERBS: the words that never change

ADVERBS: the words that never change. Before we close this lesson, I need to introduce a class of words that will give you huge relief: adverbs. I'll be direct: the adverb is the easiest class of words in the whole of Russian. I am not exaggerating, and you will see why in three minutes. What is an adverb? An adverb is a word that modifies the verb. It tells you how, when, where or how often the action happens. You use adverbs all the time in English: I read quickly (how?). We arrived today (when?). He lives here (where?). She always studies (how often?). Quickly, today, here, always: all adverbs. They attach to the verb and tell you how, when or where the action happens. The big news: the adverb is INVARIABLE. Now pay attention to this word: invariable. It means: it does not change. Ever. For any reason. Let me prove it with concrete examples. Proof 1: the adverb does not change with gender. Take the English adverb "today". Does it change if the speaker is a man or a woman? "I am happy today" is the same for both. There is no "todayess" for a woman. Russian is the same. The adverb сего́дня (today) is always сего́дня, whether the speaker is a man, a woman, a child or an adult. Proof 2: the adverb does not change with number. Take "here". Does it change if one person or several are here? "I am here. We are here." No. "Here" is "here" for one or for a thousand. Russian is the same: здесь is always здесь. Proof 3: the adverb does not change with tense. Take "yesterday". It does not become anything else when the verb changes. Russian is the same. The adverb вчера́ (yesterday) is always вчера́. What changes is the verb, not the adverb: in the past tense «читал» changes to «читала» for a woman, but вчера́ stays put. The golden rule of the adverb: an adverb is a frozen word. It does not change with gender, number, person, tense or case. It is always the same form, in any sentence, with any subject, in any context. That is why the adverb is the easiest class in Russian. While nouns, adjectives and verbs change form, adverbs stand still. If you like memorising, memorise adverbs. There are no tricks, no exceptions, no conjugation. It is the only class in Russian where you can learn a word and use it for ever without fear. Some essential adverbs. Here are the most used adverbs in everyday life; notice that all are invariable. Time. Place. Manner. How to use adverbs in sentences. The position of the adverb is flexible. Generally: an adverb of time goes before the verb or at the start of the sentence. An adverb of place goes after the verb. An adverb of manner goes after the verb. Examples follow. Notice that the adverb never changes form, whatever the sentence. Хорошо́ is always хорошо́. Сего́дня is always сего́дня. Здесь is always здесь. You do not need to think about gender, number, person or tense. Just drop the word in. Comparison with English: you already do this. In English the adverb is invariable too: I speak well. She speaks well. We speak well. They speak well. "Well" is always "well". The difference: in English many adverbs are made from adjectives by adding "-ly" (slow → slowly, quick → quickly). In Russian many adverbs are made from adjectives by changing the ending to -о (or -е): хоро́ший → хорошо́, бы́стрый → бы́стро. But that is only the origin of the adverb. Once formed, it stands still. Хорошо́ does not become anything else for a woman or for a plural. It is always хорошо́. Full stop. An important remark: adverb versus neuter adjective. Be careful not to confuse the adverb with the neuter adjective. They can have the same form but different jobs. Он хорошо́ говори́т. (He speaks well.) → хорошо́ is an adverb: it modifies the verb говори́т. Э́то хоро́шее вино́. (This is a good wine.) → хоро́шее is a neuter adjective: it modifies the noun вино́. The difference is in the job: if it modifies a verb, it is an adverb; if it modifies a noun, it is an adjective. Context makes this clear. Quick exercise. Complete with the right adverb. • 1. Я ____ чита́ю. (now) • 2. Он ____ рабо́тает. (today) • 3. Мы бу́дем ____ в Москве́. (tomorrow) • 4. Я был ____ в теа́тре. (yesterday) • 5. Она́ живёт ____. (there) • 6. Он ____ чита́ет. (here) • 7. Я ____. (at home) • 8. Она́ ____ говори́т по-ру́сски. (well) • 9. Он ____ чита́ет. (slowly) • 10. Они́ ____ рабо́тают. (always) Answer key: • 1. сейча́с • 2. сего́дня • 3. за́втра • 4. вчера́ • 5. там • 6. здесь (or тут) • 7. до́ма • 8. хорошо́ • 9. ме́дленно • 10. всегда́. Pocket summary: adverbs. • 1. An adverb is a word that modifies the verb (it says how, when, where, how often). • 2. The adverb is invariable. It does not change with gender, number, person, tense or case. • 3. "Today" is today for a man, a woman, a child, an adult. Always. • 4. "Here" is here for one person or a thousand. Always. • 5. "Well" is well for any subject. Always. • 6. If you like memorising, memorise adverbs. They are the easiest class in Russian: no conjugation, no declension, no tricks. Just use them. • 7. The most essential: сейча́с, сего́дня, за́втра, вчера́, всегда́, никогда́, здесь, там, до́ма, хорошо́, пло́хо, бы́стро, ме́дленно.

Tabela de Mutação Consonantal nos Verbos: Consonant mutation in verbs, and a summary chart of the two conjugations in the present. Some verbs change the last consonant of the stem. In the second conjugation the change usually happens only in the я form (люблю́ but лю́бишь, лю́бят). In the first conjugation (for example писа́ть) the changed consonant stays in all forms (пишу́, пи́шешь, пи́шут). English has a faint echo of this ("office" and "officer", "electric" and "electricity", where k becomes s), but in Russian it is regular and predictable.
